title: Motherhood Is Fun
author: Nadya Williams Source: mereorthodoxy.substack.com
summary: Nadya Williams offers a counter-narrative to dominant media portrayals of motherhood as burden, trap, or career penalty, arguing that modern motherhood is genuinely fun in ways that are consistently underacknowledged. She grounds the argument historically: pre-modern mothers faced cloth diaper washing by hand, child mortality before antibiotics, scarce books, and hours of food procurement that today's mothers have been freed from—making contemporary complaints about motherhood-as-drudgery historically anomalous. Her affirmative case draws from her own screen-free homeschooling household in rural Ohio, where she reads classic books, reviews Greek and Latin grammar, attends ballet, and has conversations with children who are 'some of my favorite people around.' Institute for Family Studies data is cited showing that married mothers consistently report higher happiness scores than either single women or women without children. Williams acknowledges the work without minimizing it but insists the contemporary framing—which emphasizes ambivalence and opt-out—leads women to miss joys that are only visible when you have decided, in advance, to look for them.
points: Contemporary media frames motherhood as burden, penalty, and trap—but this framing is historically anomalous: modern mothers have been freed from cloth diapers, child mortality, costly books, and hours of food procurement that past generations bore.

Screen-free, enrichment-oriented home life (classic books, languages, arts, outdoor play) produces children who are genuinely interesting conversation partners and whose development becomes a daily source of discovery.

Institute for Family Studies data shows married mothers consistently report higher happiness scores than either single women or childless women, contradicting the dominant cultural narrative about the cost of motherhood.
The fun of motherhood is only visible to those who have decided to look for it; the ambivalence-affirming framing in mainstream media pre-disposes women to miss joys that are structurally present.

Modern amenities (grocery delivery, washing machines, affordable books, medical advances) have removed most of the drudgery while leaving the joys intact—making the contemporary case for motherhood stronger, not weaker, than at any prior historical moment.
quotes: I could understand some media hand-wringing over the challenges of motherhood at a time when it required significantly more daily physical and mental labor than it does now. But it is striking to see the complaints and the constant reassurances that it is okay to be ambivalent over having (or not having) children bloom so freely in an age where the more drudgery-oriented tasks of motherhood have largely been removed from us.
My kids are some of my favorite people around—because they are genuinely fun people to be around.
I read much more since becoming a mom—not less. And, no less important, my reading is much more diverse now, because of my kids.

There is a delight in spending time together with my kids, enjoying rediscovering activities that I once loved as a child but haven't had time for since, and also seeing my kids discover their own interests and talents.
